name: Iloperidone (Fanapt)
summary: Atypical antipsychotic used for schizophrenia and acute manic or mixed episodes in bipolar I disorder. Requires slow titration to reduce dizziness and fainting risk, and it can prolong the QT interval (heart rhythm risk).
description: Fanapt (iloperidone) is a second-generation antipsychotic used in adults for schizophrenia and for acute manic or mixed episodes in bipolar I disorder. It has to be started low and increased slowly because it can cause orthostatic hypotension (lightheadedness when standing), fast heart rate, and fainting—especially early on. It can also prolong the QT interval, which raises the risk of dangerous heart rhythm problems in higher-risk patients or when combined with certain meds. Like all antipsychotics, it carries a boxed warning for increased mortality in elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis and is not approved for that use.
patient_summary: Fanapt can help stabilize psychosis or mania, but it’s not a “pop a pill and instantly feel better” medication. The build-up is intentionally slow to avoid dizziness, fainting, and heart rhythm problems. Expect early side effects to be more about lightheadedness and sleepiness than anything else. It can also raise prolactin, affect cholesterol, and cause weight gain for some people—so the plan usually includes metabolic monitoring, not just symptom check-ins.

metadata.pharmacologic_category: Atypical antipsychotic (mixed dopamine/serotonin antagonist with strong alpha-1 blockade)

primary_indications: Bipolar I Disorder: Acute manic or mixed episodes (adults)

linked_conditions.context: Used in adults for schizophrenia. Effects can begin to show within 1 to 2 weeks, with continued improvement through 4 to 6 weeks. Slow titration means it can take longer to reach a full therapeutic dose.
Used in adults for acute manic or mixed episodes in bipolar I disorder. Dose is increased over days to reduce orthostatic hypotension risk while working toward a target dose.
Not approved for dementia-related psychosis. Antipsychotics increase mortality risk in elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis.
Antipsychotics are generally not indicated for catatonia and can worsen psychosis and increase neuroleptic malignant syndrome risk in catatonic patients. Specialist involvement is recommended.

contraindications: Hypersensitivity to iloperidone or any component of the formulation (including anaphylaxis or angioedema history with this medication)

efficacy_response.patient_text: Fanapt isn’t an instant-on medication. Many people notice early changes within 1 to 2 weeks, but the more meaningful improvements often build across 4 to 6 weeks—especially because the dose has to be titrated slowly for safety.

pharmacokinetics.absorption: Well absorbed; can be taken with or without food
pharmacokinetics.onset: Schizophrenia: initial effects may be observed within 1 to 2 weeks; continued improvement through 4 to 6 weeks; slow titration delays time to therapeutic dose
pharmacokinetics.half_life: Extensive metabolizers: iloperidone ~18 hours (active metabolites ~23 to 26 hours); Poor metabolizers: iloperidone ~33 hours (active metabolites ~31 to 37 hours)
pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Hepatic via carbonyl reduction, hydroxylation (CYP2D6), and O-demethylation (CYP3A4); forms active metabolites (P88 and P95)
pharmacokinetics.excretion: Mostly as metabolites via urine and feces; <1% recovered unchanged

sections.heading: What It's Used For
sections.text: Fanapt is an atypical antipsychotic used in adults for schizophrenia and for acute manic or mixed episodes in bipolar I disorder. It’s not approved for dementia-related psychosis, and it’s generally not a go-to option for catatonia. Because it can cause orthostatic hypotension and QT prolongation, the dose has to be increased gradually and the medication choice should be individualized based on your medical history, current meds, and side effect priorities.
items: {link:condition:schizophrenia:Schizophrenia}: Hallucinations, delusions, disorganized thinking, agitation, and related functional impairment

{link:condition:bipolar-i-disorder:Bipolar I Disorder (acute mania or mixed episodes)}: Elevated or irritable mood, decreased need for sleep, racing thoughts, impulsivity, agitation, and psychosis (when present)

sections.heading: What People Feel
sections.intro: Everyone’s brain and body respond differently, but these are the patterns that come up a lot with Fanapt—especially during the slow titration phase:

quotes: I stood up and felt that head-rush thing—like I needed a second before walking.
It made me sleepy at first. Not horrible, but definitely noticeable.
I felt calm-ish, but also kind of slowed down for a bit.
items.note: This medication is intentionally titrated slowly to lower the risk of orthostatic hypotension, fast heart rate, and fainting.

quotes: The volume turned down. The thoughts weren’t as loud or sticky.
I was still me, but less revved up and less reactive.
By a few weeks in, things felt less chaotic—more manageable.
items.note: Improvement can start within 1 to 2 weeks, but fuller changes often build across 4 to 6 weeks.

quotes: My appetite shifted. I had to pay attention so it didn’t sneak up on me.
My labs changed before I felt anything—so the monitoring actually mattered.
I didn’t feel ‘sick,’ but my weight crept up faster than expected.
items.note: Fanapt can affect weight, lipids, and glucose regulation. The plan should include metabolic monitoring, not just symptom tracking.

quotes: My sex drive dipped and it was kind of annoying to talk about—but it was real.
I noticed changes that made me wonder about hormones.
I felt fine mentally, but the side effects were the trade-off.
items.note: Iloperidone can raise prolactin. If symptoms show up (sexual dysfunction, menstrual changes, galactorrhea, gynecomastia), it’s worth addressing directly—sometimes the fix is dose, sometimes it’s a switch.

items.category: Restlessness or EPS (less common, still possible)
quotes: I felt a little restless in my body—like I couldn’t fully chill.
Not full-on stiffness, but a weird inner pacing feeling.
It wasn’t dramatic, but I noticed it.
items.note: EPS rates can be similar to placebo in trials, but individual vulnerability varies—especially with higher doses or prior EPS history.

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: Fanapt is not a same-day, instant-relief medication. The timeline is shaped by two things: (1) how antipsychotics work (gradual symptom change), and (2) the fact that Fanapt requires slow titration to avoid blood pressure drops and fainting.
key_points: 2 to 4 hours: Peak blood levels after a dose
Days 1 to 7: You may feel side effects first (sleepiness, dizziness, lightheadedness) while the dose is being built
1 to 2 weeks: Early symptom shifts can start to show for some people
4 to 6 weeks: More meaningful improvement often becomes clearer with steady dosing
~18 hours (extensive metabolizers) / ~33 hours (CYP2D6 poor metabolizers): Approximate parent-drug half-life; active metabolites last longer

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.value: Gradual reduction in psychosis/mania severity over weeks
sections.text: Fanapt can reduce hallucinations, delusions, agitation, and disorganized thinking in schizophrenia, and can help calm and stabilize acute mania or mixed episodes in bipolar I disorder. The big practical detail is that it’s titrated slowly for safety—so the timeline to full benefit can feel slower than some other antipsychotics. Clinically, the goal is not just “fewer symptoms,” but better function: improved sleep-wake rhythm, less agitation, clearer thinking, and fewer crisis-level spikes.
sections.clinical_details: Initial symptom changes may be observed within 1 to 2 weeks, with continued improvement across 4 to 6 weeks. Slow titration delays reaching a full therapeutic dose, and early visits often focus on tolerability (orthostasis, sedation, heart rhythm risk) while moving toward the recommended dose range.

sections.heading: Critical Safety Information
sections.highlight: Boxed warning: increased mortality in elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis. Fanapt is not approved for dementia-related psychosis.
sections.black_box: Elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis treated with antipsychotic drugs are at an increased risk of death. Iloperidone is not approved for the treatment of patients with dementia-related psychosis.
other: QT prolongation: Fanapt can prolong the QT interval and raise the risk of dangerous arrhythmias—especially in people with congenital long QT syndrome, prior serious arrhythmias, recent MI, uncompensated heart failure, bradycardia, or low potassium/magnesium, or when combined with QT-prolonging drugs
Orthostatic hypotension and syncope: Dose must be increased gradually to reduce dizziness, fast heart rate, and fainting risk
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS): Rare but life-threatening; symptoms include fever, rigidity, confusion, and autonomic instability
Blood dyscrasias: Leukopenia/neutropenia/agranulocytosis have been reported; monitor CBC when clinically indicated and especially if risk factors exist
Cerebrovascular events in dementia: Higher rates of stroke/TIA and deaths have been seen when antipsychotics are used for dementia-related psychosis (unapproved use)
Metabolic effects: Weight gain, dyslipidemia, and hyperglycemia can occur; monitor labs and body measures
Hyperprolactinemia: Can cause sexual side effects and reproductive/hormonal symptoms
Falls risk: Somnolence + orthostasis + motor instability can increase falls, especially in older adults
Seizure risk: Use caution in patients with seizure risk factors or medications that lower seizure threshold
Catatonia caution: Antipsychotics are generally not indicated in catatonia and may worsen psychosis and increase NMS risk in catatonic patients
patient_counseling: Stand up slowly, especially during the first weeks. If you feel faint, sit or lie down right away.
Tell your clinician about any history of fainting, heart rhythm problems, heart disease, or family history of sudden cardiac death.
Avoid mixing with other meds that can prolong QT unless your prescriber has explicitly reviewed the combo.
Call urgently for chest fluttering, fainting, severe dizziness, or seizures.
Seek emergency care for fever + severe stiffness + confusion (possible NMS).
Expect metabolic monitoring (weight, glucose, lipids). This is not optional fluff—it’s safety.
If you’re older, the lowest effective dose and regular “do we still need this?” check-ins matter.
Sound-alike warning: Fanapt can be confused with Xanax—double-check the name at pickup and before dosing.

sections.heading: Side Effects
sections.summary: Most common: dizziness, drowsiness/sedation, fast heart rate, weight gain, increased prolactin, and lipid changes. Fanapt is also notable for orthostatic hypotension during titration and QT prolongation risk.
plain_language_list: Dizziness or lightheadedness (especially when standing up)
Weight gain and appetite changes (varies person to person)
Prolactin-related side effects (sexual side effects, menstrual changes, breast symptoms)

common.patient_note: This can show up early, especially during titration. If it comes with fainting, chest pain, or severe dizziness, it needs prompt medical review because of QT-related risk factors and orthostasis.

Prolactin effects can be silent until symptoms appear. If you notice sexual dysfunction, menstrual changes, galactorrhea, or gynecomastia, bring it up—there are options (dose change, switch, or targeted workup).
This is why baseline and follow-up lipid panels matter. You can feel fine while your labs drift in the wrong direction.
The range is wide because people vary. If weight is a high-priority concern, build a plan early (nutrition, activity, sleep stabilization, and monitoring).
Often tied to orthostatic hypotension. Hydration, slow position changes, and cautious titration reduce risk. This is one of the main reasons Fanapt is started low and increased gradually.
Sleepiness can be helpful if agitation is severe, but it can also interfere with function. Avoid driving or risky tasks until you know your response.
This is the headline tolerability issue early on. Falls risk is real—especially in older adults or anyone on antihypertensives.

common.incidence: Nausea/vomiting: 4% to 10%; Diarrhea: 5% to 7%; Abdominal distress: 3%
common.patient_note: Often improves as your body adjusts. If dehydration worsens dizziness, the fix may be supportive care plus a slower titration.
Hydration and sugar-free gum/lozenges can help. Persistent dryness can affect dental health over time, so it’s worth addressing.
Rates may be low, but akathisia can feel awful (inner restlessness). If you feel like you can’t sit still or your body is buzzing, don’t just power through—tell your prescriber.

serious: QT prolongation and arrhythmias: Can be life-threatening, especially with other QT-prolonging meds, electrolyte abnormalities, bradycardia, structural heart disease, or congenital long QT syndrome
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS): fever, rigidity, confusion, autonomic instability (MEDICAL EMERGENCY)
Severe orthostatic hypotension/syncope: falls, injury, and rare complications
Neutropenia/agranulocytosis: increased infection risk; discontinue if ANC <1,000/mm3 and follow WBC until recovery
Hyperglycemia: can be severe; rare cases associated with ketoacidosis or hyperosmolar coma have been reported with atypical antipsychotics as a class
Tardive dyskinesia: potentially irreversible abnormal movements; risk increases with duration, dose, and vulnerability factors
Cerebrovascular events in elderly dementia patients (unapproved use): stroke/TIA, sometimes fatal
Hypersensitivity reactions: including angioedema and anaphylaxis

sections.heading: Critical Drug Interactions
sections.intro: Fanapt interacts in two big ways: (1) heart rhythm risk (QT prolongation), and (2) metabolism (CYP2D6 and CYP3A4). It can also stack sedation and blood pressure effects with other meds.

items.with: QT-prolonging medications (certain antiarrhythmics, some antibiotics, some antidepressants, methadone, etc.)
items.risk: Additive QT prolongation increases risk of torsades de pointes and sudden cardiac death—especially if combined with electrolyte abnormalities or cardiac disease.
items.action: Avoid combinations when possible. If unavoidable, use careful risk assessment, correct potassium/magnesium, and consider ECG monitoring after dose changes or when adding QT-prolonging agents.

items.with: CYP2D6 inhibitors (examples: fluoxetine, paroxetine, bupropion, quinidine)
items.risk: Higher iloperidone exposure and greater risk of side effects (orthostasis, QT issues, sedation).
items.action: Use caution and consider lower dosing targets and slower titration, especially if the patient is also a CYP2D6 poor metabolizer.

items.with: CYP3A4 inhibitors (examples: ketoconazole, clarithromycin, some HIV/HCV antivirals)
items.risk: Higher iloperidone exposure; increased risk of adverse effects including hypotension and QT-related concerns.
items.action: Avoid when possible or adjust regimen with specialist input. Review the full med list and consider ECG monitoring in higher-risk situations.

items.with: CYP3A4 inducers (examples: carbamazepine, phenytoin, rifampin, St. John’s Wort)
items.risk: Lower iloperidone levels and reduced efficacy; symptom breakthrough or relapse risk.
items.action: Avoid if possible. If used, plan close symptom monitoring and consider switching antipsychotic rather than chasing dose in a way that destabilizes tolerability.

items.risk: More hypotension and fainting risk due to additive blood pressure lowering.
items.action: Monitor orthostatics closely during titration, adjust blood pressure meds if needed, and prioritize hydration and slow position changes.

items.with: Alcohol, sedating antihistamines, benzodiazepines, sleep meds, other CNS depressants
items.risk: Additive sedation and impaired coordination; higher falls and accident risk.
items.action: Minimize combinations when possible and counsel about driving/operating machinery until response is known.

sections.heading: Safe Discontinuation
sections.text: With chronic psychiatric illness, the decision is often “switching” rather than abruptly stopping. If Fanapt is ineffective or side effects are intolerable, a structured plan matters—both to avoid relapse and to reduce withdrawal-type reactions. If someone insists on stopping and it’s not an emergency, tapering over weeks to months is generally safer so you can spot early relapse signals and avoid rebound symptoms.
key_points: Don’t stop suddenly unless there’s a serious adverse event that requires immediate discontinuation (for example, suspected NMS).

Withdrawal/rebound symptoms can include: agitation, anxiety, diaphoresis, insomnia, irritability, GI symptoms, tremor, vertigo, dyskinesias, paresthesia, restlessness, rhinorrhea, alternating feelings of warmth and chill, myalgia, and return of psychosis.
If symptoms are returning, it can look like “withdrawal” when it’s actually early relapse—this is why a slower taper with close monitoring is useful.

Switching strategies vary: cross-titration (gradually down on old med while gradually up on new), abrupt change with gradual start of the new agent, or overlap in high-relapse-risk schizophrenia (keep current med full dose while the new med is increased, then taper the old med over 1 to 2 weeks once the new med is therapeutic).
If discontinuation is due to significant adverse effects, the risk/benefit can shift toward a faster change—this should be individualized with specialist input.

sections.heading: Dosing Information
sections.text: Fanapt dosing is built around safety: start low and increase gradually to reduce orthostatic hypotension (lightheadedness, fast heart rate, fainting). Doses are typically split into two equal doses per day. If you stop for more than a few days, you usually have to restart titration rather than jumping back to your prior dose.

adult.schizophrenia_initial: 2 mg/day PO in 2 equally divided doses (1 mg BID). If first episode psychosis, consider 1 mg/day PO in 2 equally divided doses (0.5 mg BID) because sensitivity to adverse effects can be higher.
adult.schizophrenia_titration: Beginning day 2, increase based on response/tolerability in increments no greater than 4 mg/day every ≥1 day. Monitor for orthostatic hypotension and sedation during titration.
adult.schizophrenia_typical: 12 to 24 mg/day PO in 2 equally divided doses
adult.schizophrenia_max: 24 mg/day PO in 2 equally divided doses
adult.bipolar_mania_initial: 2 mg/day PO in 2 equally divided doses (1 mg BID)
adult.bipolar_mania_day2: On day 2, may increase total daily dose based on response and tolerability to 6 mg/day PO in 2 equally divided doses
adult.bipolar_mania_titration: Starting day 3, may increase total daily dose in increments no greater than 6 mg/day every ≥1 day based on response and tolerability
adult.bipolar_mania_recommended: 24 mg/day PO in 2 equally divided doses
adult.bipolar_mania_max: 24 mg/day PO in 2 equally divided doses
adult.cyp2d6_poor_metabolizer_bipolar_mania: Initial 2 mg/day PO in 2 equally divided doses; day 2 may increase to 6 mg/day based on response/tolerability; beginning day 3 may increase total daily dose to a recommended dose of 12 mg/day PO in 2 equally divided doses.
adult.cyp2d6_poor_metabolizer_schizophrenia: Initial 2 mg/day PO in 2 equally divided doses; day 2 may increase to 4 mg/day based on response/tolerability; beginning day 3 may increase in increments of 4 mg/day every ≥1 day; recommended dosage range 6 to 12 mg/day PO in 2 equally divided doses.
adult.missed_doses_restart_rule: If dosing is interrupted for >3 days, restart the initial titration schedule rather than resuming the prior dose.
adult.administration: Administer with or without food; typically dosed BID in equal divided doses to reduce side effect burden and keep levels steadier.
adult.safety_note_orthostasis: Increase dose gradually to avoid orthostatic hypotensive effects; monitor for dizziness, tachycardia, and syncope during titration.

sections.simple_explanation: Fanapt is one of the antipsychotics where the slow build-up is part of the safety plan. The early days are about tolerability (especially dizziness/fainting risk) while you climb toward the dose that actually treats symptoms.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, Special Groups
sections.text: Fanapt has important population-specific cautions. The biggest red flag is dementia-related psychosis in older adults (boxed warning). Pregnancy and breastfeeding decisions should be individualized with shared decision-making, focusing on lowest effective dose, avoiding polytherapy when possible, and monitoring both psychiatric stability and metabolic effects.
sections.pregnancy: Class-level data for second-generation antipsychotics do not show a major overall increase in congenital malformations, but individual-agent data can be limited. Antipsychotic exposure in the third trimester can be associated with newborn EPS and/or withdrawal symptoms (agitation, feeding problems, abnormal tone, respiratory distress, somnolence, tremor). Tapering late in pregnancy to try to prevent newborn symptoms is not recommended. Untreated psychosis/mania carries serious pregnancy risks; continuing an effective medication may be appropriate when benefits outweigh risks, using the lowest effective dose and avoiding polytherapy when possible.
sections.lactation: It is not known whether iloperidone is present in human breast milk. The manufacturer does not recommend breastfeeding during iloperidone treatment. For antipsychotics as a group, infant sedation, poor feeding, irritability, motor abnormalities, and slowed development have been reported. If exposure occurs, monitor infants closely—especially premature or low birth weight infants or when other sedating drugs are used.
sections.pediatrics: Safety and efficacy for iloperidone in pediatric patients are not established in the provided information. In general, dopamine antagonists are considered higher-risk in pediatrics due to metabolic effects and movement-disorder risks, and rapid discontinuation in patients ≤18 years can be associated with emergent dystonia/dyskinesia. Specialist-led care is recommended if used.
sections.geriatrics: Avoid for behavioral problems associated with dementia or delirium unless nonpharmacologic approaches have failed and there is risk of harm to self or others. For labeled indications (such as schizophrenia), older adults may respond to the lower end of adult dosing; titrate slowly and monitor carefully. Antipsychotics are listed as potentially inappropriate in adults ≥65 due to higher stroke risk, cognitive decline, and mortality in dementia; older adults are also more vulnerable to orthostasis, falls, hyponatremia/SIADH, tardive dyskinesia, and seizures.
sections.hepatic: Mild hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh A): no adjustment typically needed. Moderate hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh B): use caution; dose adjustment may be necessary. Severe hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh C): use is not recommended.
sections.renal: No manufacturer-provided dose adjustments; renal impairment alone is unlikely to meaningfully change iloperidone pharmacokinetics. Monitor clinically, especially if dehydration or other risk factors increase orthostasis risk.
sections.cyp2d6_poor_metabolizers: Use with caution and follow the reduced dosing recommendations (lower target ranges for schizophrenia and lower recommended dose for bipolar mania) because exposure and side effects can increase with slower metabolism.

sections.heading: Clinical Monitoring
items: Adherence: Every visit—because missed doses >3 days often require restarting titration, and adherence changes can look like “med failure.”
Mental status and safety: Every visit—psychosis/mania severity, agitation, suicidality risk, and functional changes (sleep, behavior, insight).

Orthostatic vitals and pulse: Every visit (at least weekly during the first 3 to 4 weeks of treatment); repeat 4 weeks after dose changes—especially in older adults, dehydration/hypovolemia, antihypertensive use, cardiovascular disease, or cerebrovascular disease.
Sedation and alertness: Every visit—assess driving/work safety, falls risk, and daytime impairment.

ECG (as clinically indicated): Consider baseline and repeat after significant dose increases or when adding QT-prolonging meds if cardiac risk factors exist (conduction disease, congenital long QT, bradycardia, structural heart disease, family history of sudden cardiac death). Discontinue if persistent QTc >500 ms.
Electrolytes and chemistries (renal function, liver function, TSH): Annually, and sooner when clinically indicated (especially if QT risk is present or hepatic impairment exists).
CBC: As clinically indicated; monitor more frequently early in treatment if preexisting low WBC or history of drug-induced leukopenia/neutropenia.

Metabolic monitoring: Fasting plasma glucose or HbA1c at ~4 months after initiation and annually (more often if abnormal); lipid panel at ~4 months after initiation and annually (more often if abnormal).

Weight/height/BMI: Check around 8 and 12 weeks after initiation and after dose changes, then at least quarterly; consider waist circumference at baseline and annually. Consider switching antipsychotic if BMI increases by ≥1 unit and risk/benefit supports it.
EPS monitoring: Every visit; also at ~4 weeks after initiation and after dose changes; use a formal rating scale at least annually (or every 6 months if high risk).
Tardive dyskinesia monitoring: Every visit with at least annual formal screening; higher-risk patients may need formal screening every 6 months.
Prolactin: Ask about symptoms at every visit until stable; check a level if symptoms occur (menstrual changes, libido changes, gynecomastia, galactorrhea, erectile/ejaculatory dysfunction).
Falls risk: Every visit—especially during titration and in older adults.
Glucose dysregulation symptoms: Ongoing—polyuria, polydipsia, unexplained fatigue; intervene quickly if hyperglycemia suspected.

Therapeutic drug monitoring (optional, specialist use): Draw a trough (just before next dose) if needed to confirm adherence; a commonly cited reference range is 5 to 10 ng/mL with an alert level around 20 ng/mL, but dosing should be guided by clinical response rather than chasing a lab number.

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: Fanapt is available as oral tablets in multiple strengths and as titration packs designed to help patients step up doses safely during initiation.
items: Tablets (Fanapt): 1 mg, 2 mg, 4 mg, 6 mg, 8 mg, 10 mg, 12 mg
Fanapt Titration Pack A: 1 mg (2 tablets), 2 mg (2 tablets), 4 mg (2 tablets), 6 mg (2 tablets)
Fanapt Titration Pack B: 1 mg (6 tablets), 2 mg (2 tablets), 6 mg (2 tablets), 8 mg (2 tablets)
Fanapt Titration Pack C: 1 mg (4 tablets), 2 mg (2 tablets), 6 mg (2 tablets)

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: Fanapt works by blocking dopamine (especially D2/D3) and serotonin (especially 5-HT2A) receptors—this is the core antipsychotic mechanism used to reduce hallucinations, delusions, and thought disorganization. It also blocks alpha-1 adrenergic receptors strongly, which is a big reason it can cause orthostatic hypotension (dizziness/fainting when standing). It has little to no muscarinic activity, which means it’s less “anticholinergic” than some antipsychotics, but it can still cause sedation and other CNS effects via its broader receptor profile.

sections.heading: Place in Treatment Algorithm
sections.text: Fanapt can be a reasonable option for schizophrenia or acute bipolar mania when a clinician and patient are balancing symptom control against side effects like EPS and metabolic concerns—but it has a unique practical constraint: slow titration. That makes it less ideal when rapid control is required and more suitable when careful outpatient titration is feasible. It also demands extra attention to orthostasis and QT risk, so it’s best chosen intentionally (not casually) after reviewing cardiac history, electrolyte risks, and the rest of the medication list. For older adults, especially those with dementia, the risk profile changes dramatically and the boxed warning becomes central to the decision.

seo.title: Iloperidone (Fanapt): Uses, Dosing, Side Effects, QT Risk & Titration
seo.description: Fanapt (iloperidone) for schizophrenia and bipolar I mania: why titration is slow, typical dosing (12–24 mg/day), side effects (dizziness, sedation, prolactin, weight/lipids), QT prolongation risk, monitoring, and safe discontinuation.

editorial.reviewStatement: Content medically reviewed and verified against FDA prescribing information, APA clinical practice guidelines, and current peer-reviewed literature.

faqs.a: Fanapt (iloperidone) is used in adults to treat schizophrenia and to treat acute manic or mixed episodes in bipolar I disorder. It’s not approved for dementia-related psychosis.

faqs.q: Why does Fanapt have to be titrated slowly?
faqs.a: Because it can cause orthostatic hypotension—dizziness, fast heart rate, and fainting when you stand up—especially early on. Slow titration lowers that risk.

faqs.q: How long does Fanapt take to work?
faqs.a: It’s gradual. Some people notice early changes within 1 to 2 weeks, but bigger improvements often build across 4 to 6 weeks. The timeline can feel slower because the dose is intentionally increased over days for safety.

faqs.q: What are the most common Fanapt side effects?
faqs.a: Common ones include dizziness/lightheadedness, sleepiness, fast heart rate, weight gain, increased prolactin, and cholesterol/lipid changes. Nausea, diarrhea, and dry mouth can also happen—especially early.

Yes, it can prolong the QT interval. That matters most if you already have heart rhythm risk factors (congenital long QT, prior arrhythmias, recent heart attack, uncompensated heart failure, bradycardia) or if you take other QT-prolonging medications or have low potassium/magnesium.

faqs.q: Is Fanapt safe in elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis?
faqs.a: No. Antipsychotics carry a boxed warning that elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis have an increased risk of death when treated with antipsychotic drugs. Fanapt is not approved for dementia-related psychosis.

faqs.q: What happens if I miss doses of Fanapt?
faqs.a: If you miss doses for more than 3 days, you usually need to restart the initial titration schedule instead of jumping back to the previous dose. This is to reduce dizziness, fainting, and blood pressure risks.

faqs.q: Can Fanapt cause sexual side effects?
faqs.a: It can. Fanapt may raise prolactin, which can lead to decreased libido, erectile or ejaculatory problems, menstrual changes, galactorrhea, or gynecomastia. If symptoms show up, talk to your prescriber—there are options.

faqs.q: What monitoring should I expect on Fanapt?
faqs.a: Expect checks for orthostatic blood pressure/pulse during titration, and ongoing monitoring of weight/BMI, glucose (or HbA1c), and lipids. If you have cardiac risk factors or are combining QT-prolonging meds, an ECG may be used. Movement side effects (EPS and tardive dyskinesia) should be checked regularly.

Unless there’s a serious adverse event requiring immediate discontinuation, stopping suddenly is usually a bad idea. Antipsychotics are typically tapered to reduce rebound symptoms and to watch for early relapse. If you’re switching to another antipsychotic, many clinicians use cross-titration or overlap strategies depending on relapse risk.

Usually no. Antipsychotics are generally not indicated for catatonia and can worsen psychosis and increase the risk of neuroleptic malignant syndrome in catatonic patients. This is a scenario where specialist-guided care is especially important.
